current-mirrors.prompt: With β = 50 and V_A = 100 V at 1 mA, compare the base-current error and output resistance of a basic mirror and a Wilson mirror.
current-mirrors.hint: Basic: 2/β and r_o. Wilson: 2/(β² + 2β + 2) and βr_o/2.

solution.text: Basic: I_out/I_ref = 1/(1 + 0.04) → −3.8%; R_out ≈ r_o = 100 kΩ.
Wilson: error 2/2602 = 0.077%; R_out ≈ 50 × 100 kΩ/2 = 2.5 MΩ. The price is one transistor and a second V_BE of headroom at the output.

differential-amplifiers.title: How far does the current move?
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A long-tailed pair has a 2 mA tail. Find both collector currents for a differential input of 20 mV.

solution.text: 20 mV already steers 68% of the current to one side—well into the nonlinear region.

differential-amplifiers.title: Differential, common-mode, CMRR
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A pair runs from ±15 V with R_C = 5 kΩ and a 7.15 kΩ tail resistor (2 mA tail). Find the single-ended and differential-output gains, the common-mode gain and the CMRR in dB.
differential-amplifiers.hint: Each side carries 1 mA, so r_e = 25.9 Ω. Use the half circuits.

solution.text: A_d = 5000/(2 × 25.9) = 96.7 single-ended, 193 between collectors.
A_cm = −5000/(2 × 7150 + 25.9) = −0.349. CMRR = 96.7/0.349 = 277 = 48.9 dB. A current-source tail would raise it by about 50 dB.

differential-amplifiers.title: Trade gain for range
differential-amplifiers.prompt: Add 100 Ω emitter resistors to the pair of the previous problem. Find the new single-ended gain. Why would you do this?

solution.text: A_d = 5000/(2 × 125.9) = 19.9, five times lower.

The linear input range grows roughly in proportion (from about ±17 mV to well over ±50 mV for the same gain error), the gain becomes set by resistors rather than by the bias current, and offset drift from r_e matters less.

differential-amplifiers.title: Gain from the Early voltage
differential-amplifiers.prompt: A pair with a PNP current-mirror load uses transistors with V_A = 80 V (all four). What is the single-ended small-signal gain, independent of the tail current?
differential-amplifiers.hint: A_d = g_m(r_o2 ∥ r_o4) with each side at I_T/2.

solution.text: The bias current cancels. The output node is high-impedance, so a follower or a high-impedance stage must come next, or the gain collapses.

differential-amplifiers.title: Where do the millivolts come from?
differential-amplifiers.prompt: The active-loaded stage above (gain 1550) has a 2 mV V_BE mismatch. Its inputs are driven from a 10 kΩ source on one side and directly from a low-impedance source on the other; each base draws 5 µA. Estimate the output offset from each cause and suggest a fix for the second.
differential-amplifiers.hint: Bias current × source resistance acts like an input offset voltage.

solution.text: V_BE mismatch: 2 mV × 1550 ≈ 3.1 V at the output—a stage like this must be inside a feedback loop.

Bias current: 5 µA × 10 kΩ = 50 mV of input offset, about 78 V of ‘output’—it would saturate. Put a matching 10 kΩ in the other input so the bias currents cancel, leaving only the much smaller offset current.

push-pull.title: The cost of a single follower
push-pull.prompt: A single NPN follower drives ±12 V into 16 Ω from ±15 V supplies, with its emitter resistor to −15 V. What quiescent current is needed, how much supply power does it draw, and what is the efficiency at full output?
push-pull.hint: The emitter resistor must sink the peak load current at the negative peak.

solution.text: Peak load current 12/16 = 0.75 A, so I_Q ≥ 0.75 A. Supply power 2 × 15 × 0.75 = 22.5 W continuously.
Full-output load power 12²/(2 × 16) = 4.5 W: efficiency 20%, and 22.5 W of heat at idle.

push-pull.title: Efficiency and the hottest amplitude
push-pull.prompt: An ideal class B stage runs from ±20 V into 4 Ω. At 16 V peak output, find load power, supply power, efficiency and transistor dissipation. At what amplitude is dissipation greatest, and how much?
push-pull.hint: P_S = 2V_CC V_p/(πR_L); maximum dissipation at V_p = 2V_CC/π.

solution.text: P_L = 16²/8 = 32 W; P_S = 2 × 20 × 16/(4π) = 50.9 W; η = 62.8%; transistors dissipate 18.9 W.

push-pull.title: How much of the wave is lost?
push-pull.prompt: A class B stage with a ±0.6 V dead zone is driven by a 2 V peak sine. For what fraction of each cycle is the output essentially zero?

solution.text: |sin ωt| < 0.3 for ωt within sin⁻¹(0.3) = 17.5° of each zero crossing: 4 × 17.5° = 70° of 360°, about 19% of the cycle.
At 10 V peak the same dead zone occupies only 4 × 3.4° ≈ 4% of the cycle, which is why crossover distortion is worst for small signals.

push-pull.title: A V_BE multiplier for Darlington outputs
push-pull.prompt: An output stage uses Darlington drivers on both sides, so the bias must span four base–emitter drops of about 0.65 V each. Design a V_BE multiplier and find its temperature coefficient.

solution.text: Need 2.6 V = 0.65(1 + R₂/R₁), so R₂/R₁ = 3: e.g. R₁ = 1 kΩ, R₂ = 3 kΩ, usually with a trimmer for adjustment.
Its voltage falls 4 × 2.1 = 8.4 mV/°C, matching the four junctions it compensates—provided it is mounted where it sees their temperature.

push-pull.title: Current limit and the short-circuit dilemma
push-pull.prompt: An output stage limits current with a 0.33 Ω emitter resistor and a sensing transistor that turns on at 0.6 V. What is the current limit? With the output shorted, what does the conducting output transistor dissipate on ±15 V supplies?
push-pull.hint: The sensing transistor clamps the drop across the resistor.

solution.text: I_limit = 0.6/0.33 = 1.8 A.

Shorted, the transistor has nearly 15 V across it at 1.8 A: about 27 W, which a small heat sink cannot sustain. Foldback limiting, which reduces the limit as the output voltage falls, or a fuse/thermal shutdown is needed.

darlington.title: Composite β
darlington.prompt: A Darlington uses β₁ = 100 and β₂ = 40. Find the composite current gain and the base current needed for 2 A in the active region.

solution.text: β = 4000 + 140 = 4140; I_B = 2 A/4140 = 0.48 mA.

darlington.title: Input impedance
darlington.prompt: That Darlington is used as an emitter follower driving an 8 Ω load. Ignoring r_e, what impedance does its input present?
darlington.hint: Multiply the load by the composite (β + 1).

solution.text: About 4141 × 8 Ω ≈ 33 kΩ, so a source of a few kilohms can drive a loudspeaker through it.

darlington.title: The cost of the extra V_BE
darlington.prompt: A load draws 3 A through a saturated switch. Compare dissipation for a Darlington at V_CE = 0.9 V and a single hard-driven transistor at 0.2 V. What base drive does the single transistor need with β = 30 and twofold overdrive?

solution.text: Darlington: 0.9 × 3 = 2.7 W (heat sink needed). Single transistor: 0.2 × 3 = 0.6 W.
Single transistor drive: 2 × 3/30 = 0.2 A of base current—which itself needs a driver transistor. This is the tradeoff a Darlington package makes for you.

darlington.title: Why the resistor across the output base
darlington.prompt: A Darlington’s driver leaks 1 µA at high temperature, and the output transistor has β = 40. Without a bleeder, how much collector current flows when the pair should be off? What does a 1 kΩ bleeder from Q₂’s base to emitter do?
darlington.hint: Q₁’s leakage becomes Q₂’s base current.

solution.text: Without the bleeder the leakage is amplified: roughly 40 µA, plus Q₁’s own share—small here, but larger at higher temperature and with higher-β devices.
The 1 kΩ bleeder carries the leakage with only 1 mV across it, far below Q₂’s turn-on voltage, so Q₂ stays off. It also gives Q₂’s stored base charge a path at turn-off, speeding release.

darlington.title: Thermal stability of the bias
darlington.prompt: An output stage’s bias network must track the input V_BE of its output devices. Compare the temperature coefficient of the input voltage of a Darlington and of a Sziklai pair.
darlington.hint: Count how many junctions lie between the input terminal and the output emitter.

solution.text: Darlington: two junctions, about −4.2 mV/°C, both partly in the hot output device.
Sziklai: one junction, the small driver’s, about −2.1 mV/°C, and that transistor does not heat itself much. The Sziklai’s bias is easier to stabilize—one reason it is favored in output stages.

bootstrapping.title: How big does it look?
bootstrapping.prompt: A 100 kΩ resistor is bootstrapped by a follower with gain 0.98. What is its effective value? What if the gain is 0.995?

solution.text: G = 0.98: 100 kΩ/0.02 = 5 MΩ. G = 0.995: 20 MΩ. The result is very sensitive to how close G is to 1.

bootstrapping.title: A driven shield
bootstrapping.prompt: A 1 m cable with 100 pF of capacitance connects a 10 MΩ source to an amplifier. Find the low-pass corner. If the shield is driven by a follower with G = 0.995, what is the new corner?

solution.text: Unguarded: f = 1/(2π × 10 MΩ × 100 pF) = 159 Hz.
Guarded: C_eff = 0.5 pF, so f = 32 kHz, 200 times higher.

bootstrapping.title: What limits the bootstrapped follower?
bootstrapping.prompt: A bootstrapped follower has β = 200, R_E = 4.7 kΩ and a bias divider whose parallel resistance is 47 kΩ, connected to the emitter through the bootstrap capacitor. Estimate the maximum input impedance, ignoring r_e and assuming the bootstrapped R₃ is huge.
bootstrapping.hint: The divider now loads the emitter; the base sees (β + 1) times the total emitter load.

solution.text: Emitter load: 4.7 kΩ ∥ 47 kΩ = 4.27 kΩ. Z_in ≈ 201 × 4.27 kΩ ≈ 860 kΩ. A Darlington follower, or a current source instead of R_E, would raise it further.

bootstrapping.title: Negative gain shrinks impedance
bootstrapping.prompt: A 100 kΩ resistor connects the input and output of an inverting amplifier with gain −9. What resistance does the input see through it? What does this have to do with the Miller effect?

solution.text: Z_eff = 100 kΩ/(1 − (−9)) = 10 kΩ.
A capacitor in the same position looks 10 times larger. That is the Miller effect (Chapter 41): the bootstrapping formula with a negative gain.

bootstrapping.title: A bootstrapped collector resistor
bootstrapping.prompt: A common-emitter stage at 1 mA has its collector load split; the 5 kΩ section next to the collector is bootstrapped by a follower with G = 0.98 and input impedance 500 kΩ. The transistor’s r_o is 100 kΩ. Estimate the effective load and the voltage gain.
bootstrapping.hint: The bootstrapped resistor looks R/(1 − G); combine it in parallel with the follower’s input and r_o.

solution.text: Bootstrapped resistor: 5 kΩ/0.02 = 250 kΩ. Effective load: 250 k ∥ 500 k ∥ 100 k = 62.5 kΩ.
Gain ≈ g_m × 62.5 kΩ = 38.7 mS × 62.5 kΩ ≈ 2400, versus g_m × 10 kΩ ≈ 390 for a plain 10 kΩ load. Now r_o, not the resistor, is the limit.

current-sharing.title: An exponential split
current-sharing.prompt: Two paralleled transistors with no ballast share 3 A. One needs 8 mV less V_BE than the other at equal current. Ignoring heating, how is the current split?

solution.text: Ratio e8/25.85 = 1.363. I₁ = 3 × 1.363/2.363 = 1.73 A, I₂ = 1.27 A.

current-sharing.title: Size the resistors
current-sharing.prompt: For the same pair at 1.5 A each, choose emitter resistors that keep the static imbalance below 5%. What does each resistor dissipate?

solution.text: Need I·R_E + V_T ≥ 8 mV/0.05 = 160 mV, so I·R_E ≥ 134 mV and R_E ≥ 0.089 Ω → 0.1 Ω.
Dissipation 1.5² × 0.1 = 0.23 W each; use 0.5 W or larger resistors.

current-sharing.title: Stable or not?
current-sharing.prompt: Each device carries 1 A at V_CE = 20 V on a heat sink giving 3 °C/W per device. Compute the electro-thermal loop gain without ballast and with 0.33 Ω.
current-sharing.hint: G = θV_CE I(2.1 mV/°C)/(V_T + I R_E).

solution.text: Without ballast: 3 × 20 × 1 × 0.0021/0.0259 = 4.9: hogging (or runaway) is certain.

current-sharing.title: Minimum ballast for margin
current-sharing.prompt: For the conditions of the previous problem, find the smallest emitter resistor that keeps the loop gain at or below 0.5.

solution.text: V_T + R_E ≥ 0.252 Ω, so R_E ≥ 0.226 Ω → 0.27 Ω (G ≈ 0.43).
If the same pair must also survive 30 V, the loop gain rises by 1.5: recheck, or use a better heat sink.

current-sharing.title: Do MOSFETs need ballast?
current-sharing.prompt: Paralleled MOSFETs are often said to share current naturally. When is that true, and when is it not?
current-sharing.hint: How does R_DS(on) change with temperature, and what happens in linear operation at low gate drive?

solution.text: In switching service, fully enhanced, R_DS(on) rises with temperature, so a hotter device carries less current: sharing is self-correcting.

In linear operation at low gate drive (below the zero-temperature-coefficient point), drain current rises with temperature at fixed V_GS, exactly like a BJT. Linear MOSFET stages, such as electronic loads, still need source resistors or individual control loops.

miller-effect.title: From f_T to capacitance
miller-effect.prompt: A transistor runs at 2 mA with f_T = 300 MHz, C_μ = 3 pF and β = 150. Find C_π and f_β.

solution.text: g_m = 77.4 mS; C_π + C_μ = 77.4 mS/(2π × 300 MHz) = 41.1 pF, so C_π ≈ 38 pF.
f_β = 300 MHz/150 = 2 MHz: the current gain is already falling well below f_T.

miller-effect.title: Two picofarads become hundreds
miller-effect.prompt: An inverting stage has gain −120 and a 4 pF capacitance from input to output. What capacitance does the input see from it?

solution.text: 4 pF × 121 = 484 pF.

miller-effect.title: Predict the corner
miller-effect.prompt: A common-emitter stage runs at 0.5 mA (β = 100) with R_C = 20 kΩ, driven from 2 kΩ, with C_π = 8 pF and C_μ = 3 pF. Estimate its −3 dB frequency.
miller-effect.hint: g_m R_C sets the Miller multiplier; the source sees R_s ∥ r_π.

miller-effect.title: What the cascode buys
miller-effect.prompt: Convert the stage of the previous problem to a cascode. Estimate the new input capacitance and input pole. What new limit appears?

solution.text: C_in ≈ C_π + 2C_μ = 8 + 6 = 14 pF; input pole ≈ 1/(2π × 1.44 kΩ × 14 pF) ≈ 7.9 MHz, 84 times higher.
Now the output pole, R_C = 20 kΩ with C_μ of Q₂ plus wiring and load capacitance (say 5 pF total), at about 1.6 MHz, sets the bandwidth. The cascode moved the bottleneck from input to output.

miller-effect.title: The Miller plateau
miller-effect.prompt: A transistor switch is driven with 0.2 mA of base current and has C_μ = 3 pF. How fast can its collector slew, and how long does a 10 V transition take at that rate?
miller-effect.hint: dV/dt ≈ I_B/C_μ during the active-region part of the transition.

solution.text: dV/dt ≈ 0.2 mA/3 pF = 67 V/µs; 10 V takes about 0.15 µs.
Doubling the base drive halves the transition time, but storage time at turn-off grows with overdrive—the two goals conflict.
